title: Thread Embroidery vs Chikankari vs Sequin Work: How to Tell Them Apart
excerpt: Thread embroidery vs chikankari vs sequin work: what each one is, how to spot it in a photo or in hand, where to wear it and how to care for it.
body:
Thread embroidery uses coloured threads to build raised floral or geometric designs, chikankari is fine, mostly tone-on-tone white work from Lucknow on sheer fabric, and sequin work adds small shiny discs for sparkle. Each one looks different up close, suits a different occasion and needs slightly different care. Here is how to tell them apart before you buy, and how to keep them looking new.

## What each technique actually is

**Thread embroidery** is the broadest family. Coloured cotton, silk or rayon threads are stitched onto the fabric to create flowers, vines, birds or borders. It can be done by hand or by machine, and you will see it on yokes, necklines, sleeves and hems. It is the everyday hero of Indian wear because it adds colour and texture without weight.

**Chikankari** is a specific hand embroidery tradition from Lucknow. Classic chikan work is white thread on white or pastel muslin, mulmul, georgette or cotton, though coloured threads are now common too. It uses dozens of named stitches, including tiny shadow work done from the back of the fabric, so the motifs look soft and almost see-through.

**Sequin work** stitches small metallic or plastic discs (sequins) onto the fabric, often combined with thread outlines. It is all about shine and catches light beautifully in the evening.

## How to spot the difference

Online photos can be confusing, so zoom in and look for these clues.

| Feature | Thread embroidery | Chikankari | Sequin work |
|---|---|---|---|
| Colour | Often multicolour or contrast | Usually tone-on-tone, pastel or white | Metallic, silver, gold or coloured shine |
| Texture | Slightly raised, smooth satin fill | Fine, delicate, some shadow effect | Raised, glittery, catches light |
| Base fabric | Cotton, silk, georgette, flex cotton | Sheer muslin, mulmul, georgette, cotton | Cotton, georgette, net, organza |
| Feel | Soft to medium | Very light | Slightly stiff where sequins sit |
| Best for | Daily wear to festive | Summer, day events, office | Evening parties, sangeet, Diwali |

A quick test in hand: turn the piece inside out. Hand chikankari shows small, slightly uneven knots and shadow stitches. Machine thread embroidery looks very even with a backing layer or tidy rows of stitching. Sequin work has thread anchoring each disc, and you can feel tiny bumps on the reverse.

## Where to wear each one

Thread embroidery is the most versatile. A cotton kurta set with a floral yoke can go from a family lunch to a temple visit. Our [Plum Purple Embroidered Cotton Suit Set](/products/plum-purple-embroidered-cotton-3-piece-suit/) is a good example, with pink rose embroidery on the yoke that adds colour without fuss.

Chikankari shines in warm weather and daytime events: summer brunches, baby showers, Eid lunches and office wear. Its quiet elegance works best when you keep jewellery minimal.

Sequin work belongs to the evening. It glows under warm lights at a Diwali party or sangeet. If you want sparkle that still breathes, a sequin embroidered cotton set is a smart middle path. Many outfits mix techniques. ## Caring for embroidery, chikankari and sequins

All three last for years with gentle care.

1. **Wash inside out.** This protects the raised stitches and sequins from rubbing.
2. **Cold water, mild detergent.** Hand wash or use a delicate cycle in a mesh bag. Avoid bleach and strong stain removers on coloured threads.
3. **Do not wring.** Press water out with a towel, then dry flat or on a hanger in the shade.
4. **Iron from the back.** Place the embroidered area face down on a soft towel and iron the reverse on medium heat. Never iron directly over sequins.
5. **Store with care.** Fold sequin pieces with a cotton cloth or tissue between layers so discs do not snag other fabric. Keep chikankari away from direct sunlight, which can yellow white thread over time.

For heavy sequin or delicate chikankari on georgette, dry cleaning a few times a year is a safe choice.

## Choosing the right one for you

Ask yourself three questions: Where will I wear it? How warm will it be? How much shine do I want? For everyday and work, choose thread embroidery or chikankari on cotton. For festive evenings, go for sequins or a mix. If you are between sizes, a [custom fit](/custom-stitched-indian-suits-made-to-measure/) piece stitched to your bust, waist, hip and height makes even simple embroidery look polished.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is chikankari a type of thread embroidery?**
Yes. Chikankari is a specific hand thread embroidery style from Lucknow, known for fine, mostly tone-on-tone stitches on light fabrics.

**Does sequin work feel scratchy?**
It can feel slightly firm where the sequins sit, which is why a soft lining or a cotton base helps. Most sequin kurtas are lined at the yoke.

**Can I machine wash an embroidered kurta?**
Many cotton embroidered pieces handle a gentle cycle inside a mesh bag in cold water. Hand washing is kinder and makes the embroidery last longer.

**Which is best for a summer wedding guest look?**
Thread embroidery or chikankari on cotton or georgette. Add a sequin dupatta if you want a little evening shine.
